newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin has little to celebrate on 66th birthday.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin has little to celebrate on 66th birthday.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin turns 66 on Saturday, but persistent health worries leave him with little to celebrate.
Under pressure from political rivals to cede power or give it up altogether, Yeltsin is having trouble proving that he is fit to rule over Russia's 150 million people.
Doctors say he is recovering from the pneumonia which struck three weeks ago. In early November he had a quintuple heart bypass operation.

But there will be no big party for his birthday, which his spokesman, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, said would be a family affair, spent in one of the residences outside Moscow where he has been convalescing almost continuously since being re-elected in July.
"Maybe some of Boris Nikolayevich's friends will come," Yastrzhembsky added.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who flies home to Moscow from the World Economic Forum in Switzerland on Saturday, said he would visit Yeltsin with a bouquet of flowers and a gift.
"Let us all wish him a speedy recovery...Anyone takes time to get over pneumonia," he said at the gathering of political and business leaders in Davos.
"He's gaining strength with every passing day and he's actively working in the Kremlin," Chernomyrdin later told CNN television, speaking through an interpreter.
Brushing off charges that Yeltsin was unfit to rule, Chernomyrdin said his recovery would soon be evident.
"Soon there will be no basis for such speculation and such doubts. He's fully in control, political and state control and everybody will soon see that he's fit and able," he said.
On Sunday French President Jacques Chirac will arrive in Moscow to meet Yeltsin, becoming the first Western leader to see him since he was taken to hospital with pneumonia on January 8.
In a clear bid to draw attention away from Yeltsin's health, Russian Public Television said the short visit -- just two hours -- "is explained partly by unsolved problems in France".
Yeltsin visited the Kremlin on Friday for the third time since his latest illness and his spokesman said sent tough messages to his domestic rivals and the West on his behalf.

Yasztrzhembsky said Yeltsin had reiterated Russia's opposition to NATO expansion in a meeting with Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and that the president was firmly against proposals to change the consitution to dilute his vast powers.

"The president cannot agree with such proposals," Yastrzhembsky said. "In his opinion the constitution...has shown it can work, played and still plays an important stabilising role in society," he added.

The North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's plans to issue invitations to some of Moscow's former Warsaw Pact allies in July and pressing economic problems at home have fuelled charges that Russia needs a stronger man at the helm.

Asked if Yeltsin was able to handle state affairs while he, his number two, was out of the country, Chernomyrdin said: "Yes, he can and he is doing it...If there had been any doubt, and if there had been any problem, I would not have come to Davos."
